<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_leqno">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans</h1>
<span class="ltx_pubnotes ltx_pubnotes_meta"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_doi"><span class="ltx_note_name">DOI: </span><a href="https://doi.org/XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX">XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX</a></span><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_conference"><span class="ltx_note_name">Conference: </span>arXiv; 2026; </span><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_isbn"><span class="ltx_note_name">ISBN: </span>978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2026/07</span></span></span>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Evonne Ng Siwei Zhang Zhang Chen Michael Zollhoefer Alexander Richard
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_institution">Meta Reality Labs</span>, <span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_city">Redmond</span>, <span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_state">WA</span>, <span id="id4" class="ltx_text ltx_affiliation_country">USA</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">2026</div>

<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure ltx_teaserfigure"><img src="2602.18432v1/teaser.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/126;" width="476" height="126" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Our method generates full-body 3D motion for a virtual agent that is spatially aware of the user while engaging in a conversation.
Given the user’s floor-projected head trajectory and dyadic audio, we generate the agent’s complete 3D motion.
Trajectory colors indicate time: blue <math id="S0.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> green (user) and yellow <math id="S0.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> red (agent). See <a href="https://evonneng.github.io/sarah/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a> for results.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">As embodied agents become central to VR, telepresence, and digital human applications, their motion must go beyond speech-aligned gestures: agents should turn toward users, respond to their movement, and maintain natural gaze. Current methods lack this spatial awareness.
We close this gap with the first real-time, fully causal method for spatially-aware conversational motion, deployable on a streaming VR headset.
Given a user’s position and dyadic audio, our approach produces full-body motion that aligns gestures with speech while orienting the agent according to the user.
Our architecture combines a causal transformer-based VAE with interleaved latent tokens for streaming inference and a flow matching model conditioned on user trajectory and audio.
To support varying gaze preferences, we introduce a gaze scoring mechanism with classifier-free guidance to decouple learning from control: the model captures natural spatial alignment from data, while users can adjust eye contact intensity at inference time.
On the Embody 3D dataset, our method achieves state-of-the-art motion quality at over 300 FPS—3<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than non-causal baselines—while capturing the subtle spatial dynamics of natural conversation.
We validate our approach on a live VR system, bringing spatially-aware conversational agents to real-time deployment. See our <a href="https://evonneng.github.io/sarah/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a> for details.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Embodied conversational agents are becoming central to immersive applications—from virtual reality companions and telepresence avatars to social robots and digital humans.
For these agents to feel truly present, speech alone is not enough.
Consider interacting with an agent that only stares forward as you walk around it, or an agent that wanders off as you are mid-sentence.
Such behavior immediately breaks the illusion of presence.
Humans naturally turn toward their conversational partners, shift posture as they move, and modulate gaze to signal engagement.
Moreover, comfort in levels of eye contact vary widely—shaped by personal preference, social context, and cultural norms.
For virtual agents to replicate this behavior and appear humanlike, their motion must be both <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spatially aware</em> and <em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">controllable</em>—orienting toward the user while adapting gaze to individual preferences.
Current methods, however, focus on conversational contexts in isolation, producing agents that lack situated reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We present a method for generating full-body motion for a virtual agent that responds to both the conversation and the user’s spatial movement—all in real-time.
Achieving such motion requires satisfying four criteria simultaneously.
First, it must be <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">conversationally appropriate</em>—gestures should align naturally with speech.
Second, it must be <em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spatially aware</em>—the agent should orient toward and react to the user’s movement.
Third, it must be <em id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">controllable</em>—gaze engagement should be adjustable to suit different contexts and preferences.
Fourth, it must be <em id="S1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">real-time</em>—generation must be causal and streaming, with no access to future information.
Achieving all four remains an open challenge: state-of-the-art methods either ignore spatial context, require non-causal access to future frames, or run far below real-time speeds.
We present the first method to close this gap.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing gesture generation methods are predominantly monadic: they synthesize motion for a single speaker conditioned on audio or text, with no awareness of an interlocutor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nyatsanga et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexanderson et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
The few dyadic methods that exist typically assume stationary, forward-facing participants—mimicking video calls rather than dynamic, in-person interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
Moreover, popular state-of-the-art generative models are often too slow for real-time deployment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2022</a>)</cite> or require non-causal access to future frames <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexanderson et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, precluding streaming inference.
Compounding this, existing dyadic datasets lack the spatial dynamics needed to learn reactive behavior.
As a result, generated agents remain stationary and rigidly face one another—lacking the fluid spatial dynamics of real conversation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our key insight is to decouple learning from control: we learn the natural distribution of spatial alignment from data, capturing gaze behaviors from sustained eye contact to deliberate aversion, then apply a lightweight guidance mechanism at inference to calibrate orientation based on user preference.
This separation allows the model to generate motion that is both naturalistic (drawn from the learned distribution) and controllable (steered toward a desired gaze intensity).
To achieve this, we propose a real-time, causal architecture built on two core components.
First, a causal transformer-based VAE compresses motion into a temporally-strided latent sequence, with interleaved latent tokens enabling streaming inference without sacrificing temporal coherence.
Second, a flow matching model generates motion in this latent space, conditioned on the user’s trajectory and both speakers’ audio.
For fine-grained control, we introduce a gaze guidance mechanism based on classifier-free guidance, allowing users to modulate eye contact intensity at inference.
Underpinning these components is a fully Euclidean motion representation that improves training stability and enables precise end-effector control.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on the Embody 3D dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">McLean et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, the first to capture realistic proxemics in dynamic spatial interactions.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art motion quality while running at over 300 FPS, outperforming non-causal baselines (MDM, A2P) that are 3<math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> slower.
Notably, we match the gaze alignment of non-causal methods without access to future user positions, demonstrating that reactive spatial behavior can be learned causally.
The generated motion is also controllable: users can modulate eye contact intensity at inference to suit their preferences.
We deploy on a real-time avatar system, confirming viability for production.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, we present the first real-time system for spatially-aware conversational motion, enabling virtual agents to participate in dynamic interactions.
Our approach combines a causal transformer-based VAE with interleaved latent tokens for streaming inference, a Euclidean surface-point representation for stable training and precise end-effector control, and a classifier-free gaze guidance mechanism for user-adjustable eye contact.
We achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Embody 3D dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">McLean et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and successfully deploy our method on a real-time avatar system.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18432v1/method.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/203;" width="476" height="203" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>. </span><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Given the user’s 3D position and dyadic conversational audio, our model generates 3D motion that is conversationally and spatially aware (left).
We use a fully causal transformer-based VAE with interleaved latent tokens at a fixed temporal stride; both encoder and decoder employ causal attention, where each <math id="S1.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> token attends only to preceding frames and earlier latents (center).
These latents are passed to a transformer-based flow matching model that also uses causal masking and optionally accepts a gaze score for controlling the agent’s eye contact (right).
Our lightweight architecture enables real-time, autoregressive streaming without distillation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Related work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>Gestural motion generation.</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Most prior work on gestural motion generation has focused on single-person, co-speech gesture synthesis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nyatsanga et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, generating gestures that align with speaker audio.
Early methods employed recurrent neural networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghorbani et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and feed-forward architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kucherenko et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ginosar et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
More recent approaches use autoregressive transformers to produce vector-quantized motion tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yi et al., 2023</a>)</cite> that decode into continuous motion.
Conditional diffusion models have also become prominent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexanderson et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
Beyond audio, recent work has investigated text- and semantics-based conditioning for stylized gesture generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, all of these works notably focus only on speakers in monadic settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>Proxemics in interpersonal communication</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Oculesics (eye gaze and contact <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kendon, 1967</a>)</cite>) and proxemics (interpersonal distance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Argyle and Dean, 1965</a>)</cite>) play crucial roles in regulating turn-taking, signaling attention, and communicating intent.
These signals have been used as priors for predicting social formations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alahi et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, trajectory forecasting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, egocentric pose estimation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, social behavior analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Treuille et al., 2006</a>)</cite>, and activity recognition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pellegrini et al., 2010</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bagautdinov et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang and Kitani, 2014</a>)</cite>. Unlike methods that use oculesic and proxemic information as priors, we directly predict these signals.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-grained gaze and head motion modeling has been studied for dyadic conversational motion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahuja et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
However, many focus on forward-facing video calls where proxemic information is lost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or use datasets where dyadic pairs remain stationary <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahuja et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
Due to scarce datasets capturing global proxemics, recent approaches leverage LLMs to reason about proxemic cues via language.
For example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> uses an LLM for high-level gaze, proxemics, and pose guidance in dyadic interactions, while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Subramanian et al., 2024</a>)</cite> employs an LLM to refine poses of closely interacting individuals.
In contrast, we adopt a supervised approach to directly learn fine-grained proxemic information.
Closely related, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joo et al., 2019</a>)</cite> addresses gaze and turn-taking prediction but decomposes the problem into sub-tasks without full-body locomotion.
This is the first work to explicitly model fine-grained proxemics in dynamic, interactive dyadic conversations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3. </span>Realtime causal generative modeling.</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances in generative motion synthesis have focused on acausal methods, <em id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>vanilla diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tevet et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexanderson et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which require both past and future context and are unsuitable for real-time applications.
To address this, some approaches combine vector-quantization (VQ) with causal transformers for fast, autoregressive generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More recently, diffusion models have been adapted for causal generation via conditioning on past frames <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> or diffusion forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. However, these still require multiple evaluation steps, making them slower than real-time. The video diffusion community has adopted distillation to compress multi-step models into single-step models for real-time streaming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kodaira et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Motivated by these advances, we introduce an autoregressive, single-step flow-based model for real-time motion streaming.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a user and AI agent in conversation, our goal is to generate the agent’s motion conditioned on both individuals’ audio and the user’s motion.
Let <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D_{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D_{x}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D_{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D_{x}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the motion sequences of the agent and user respectively, where <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the sequence length and <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> is the motion dimension.
In headset-based systems, full body pose is often unavailable while head position is always accessible.
We therefore condition only on the user’s floor projected head position <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 2}</annotation></semantics></math>, computed as the midpoint between the left and right eyes and projected to the ground.
Let <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐛</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the audio features of agent and user, where <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is the audio dimension.
We model the generation as:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}=\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{p}_{y},\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐛</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}=\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{p}_{y},\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> is our generative model. For audio conditioning, we extract HuBERT features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hsu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> from each audio stream to obtain <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐚</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐛</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{b}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18432v1/representation.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/236;" width="476" height="236" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>. </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We represent each joint <math id="S3.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> as a 3D icosahedron.
The centroid of the vertices yields the global position <math id="S3.F3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝚷</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, and we recover the global orientation <math id="S3.F3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝛀</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> via SVD against a reference icosahedron.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Motion Representation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Traditionally, human motion is represented by local joint rotations <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> with root transforms <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(R,\mathbf{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐭</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(R,\mathbf{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Many methods predict <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(R,\mathbf{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐭</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(R,\mathbf{t})</annotation></semantics></math> directly, using forward kinematics and linear blend skinning to obtain meshes <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times V\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times V\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We find that a fully Euclidean representation leads to faster convergence and more stable training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To avoid error propagation from local rotations, we encode each joint <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> as a 3D icosahedron: the centroid of its 12 vertices yields world-space position <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝚷</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, while SVD against a reference icosahedron recovers orientation <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝛀</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
Each pose is thus represented as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times 12\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times 12\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of joints.
We additionally include mesh <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> as a shell around the joints to capture surface geometry.
To prevent unbounded drift, we normalize rotation and translation with respect to the first frame, aligning the agent at the origin facing the <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis at <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t{=}1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t{=}1</annotation></semantics></math>.
As shown in Tab. <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.5. Dyadic conversational dataset ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, this representation leads to improved performance over traditional joint-angle parameterizations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Causal Transformer-based VAE</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a causal VAE architecture to support streaming inference.
Unlike typical transformer VAEs that place global latent tokens at sequence start (enabling bidirectional attention), we interleave latent tokens at a fixed temporal stride <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Concretely, the encoder <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> receives input ordered as:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(2)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(\mathbf{x}_{1:s},\,\mu_{1},\,\sigma_{1},\,\mathbf{x}_{s+1:2s},\,\mu_{2},\,\sigma_{2},\,\ldots)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{x}_{1:s},\,\mu_{1},\,\sigma_{1},\,\mathbf{x}_{s+1:2s},\,\mu_{2},\,\sigma_{2},\,\ldots),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the mean and variance tokens for block <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{z}</annotation></semantics></math> is the latent dimension.
We apply causal self-attention: each frame attends only to past frames, and each <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{k}/\sigma_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{k}/\sigma_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> token attends to preceding frames and earlier latent tokens.
The decoder <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> mirrors this pattern.
See Fig. <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for an overview.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We optimize the VAE with reconstruction and KL losses:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(3)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}}=\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\phi}(z_{k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:ks})\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\big)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>VAE</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em">+</mo><mi>β</mi><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><mi>KL</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0.337em">∥</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}}=\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\phi}(z_{k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:ks})\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\big),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="q_{\phi}(z_{k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:ks})=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\phi}(z_{k}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1:ks})=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> is the approximate posterior, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is the KL weight, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=T/s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=T/s</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of blocks, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{x}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{x}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the reconstruction, and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the sampled latent for block <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>.
After training, we use the encoder to obtain the latent sequence <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Motion Generator</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt a transformer-based flow matching model for real-time, causal motion generation.
Flow matching transports samples from noise <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})</annotation></semantics></math> to data by predicting a velocity field <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{c})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>τ</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{c})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> is flow time, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}^{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>τ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}^{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> is the interpolated latent, and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes conditioning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We condition on the user’s head position <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> and both audio streams <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐛</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, predicting the agent’s latent <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
At flow time <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, we form:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(4)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}^{\tau}=\tau\mathbf{z}+(1-\tau)\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\quad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>τ</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐳</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}^{\tau}=\tau\mathbf{z}+(1-\tau)\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\quad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">We concatenate <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}^{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>τ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}^{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> with conditioning <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}=[\mathbf{p}_{y};\mathbf{a};\mathbf{b}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐜</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>𝐛</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}=[\mathbf{p}_{y};\mathbf{a};\mathbf{b}]</annotation></semantics></math> along the channel dimension, applying modality-specific positional encodings.
During training, we enforce classifier free guidance dropping each modality independently with a 5 percent probability.
The flow timestep <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is injected via adaptive layer normalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite>.
Using <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>-prediction, we train:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(5)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\mathbf{z}}\big[\|\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{z}^{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}\big]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>flow</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐳</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>τ</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐳</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\mathbf{z}}\big[\|\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{z}^{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}\big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For real-time streaming, we enforce strict causality via causal attention masking.
At inference, we generate motion autoregressively by maintaining a history buffer of previously predicted latents.
Rather than conditioning on past motion explicitly—which led to mode collapse—we enforce temporal consistency through imputation.
Given the predicted history <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{1:k-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{1:k-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute the corresponding noisy latents via Eq. <a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.3. Motion Generator ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and sample fresh noise for the remaining sequence.
At each denoising step, we replace the noisy history tokens with their imputed values before proceeding.
After denoising, we append the newly predicted latent to the history buffer and slide forward by one block.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4. </span>Controllable Gaze Guidance</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Eye contact is a key non-verbal cue: more signals engagement, while less may indicate reserve.
However, appropriate eye contact varies widely—depending on preference, social context, and cultural norms.
This variability motivates making gaze behavior explicitly controllable at inference time.
While conditioning on user position enables plausible reactive motion, it restricts output to the gaze distribution in training data (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5. Dyadic conversational dataset ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>).
To provide finer control, we introduce a tunable gaze guidance mechanism that modulates eye contact intensity based on user preference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18432v1/gaze_both.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/223;" width="476" height="223" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>. </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Our training data spans a wide range of gaze behaviors, from sustained eye contact to complete gaze aversion (left).
To enable controllable gaze at inference, we compute a gaze score <math id="S3.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.F4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{d}_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐝</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{d}_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> is the agent’s facing direction and <math id="S3.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{d}_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐝</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{d}_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> points toward the user (right).
The score approaches <math id="S3.F4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> when facing the user directly and <math id="S3.F4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> when facing away.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We encode gaze based on head orientation relative to user position (Fig. <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.4. Controllable Gaze Guidance ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
Let <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{f},h_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{f},h_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the front and back of the agent’s head.
We define the agent’s facing direction as:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(6)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{x}=\frac{h_{f}-h_{b}}{\|h_{f}-h_{b}\|}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{x}=\frac{h_{f}-h_{b}}{\|h_{f}-h_{b}\|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">and the direction toward the user as:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(7)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{y}=\frac{p_{y}-h_{b}}{\|p_{y}-h_{b}\|}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{y}=\frac{p_{y}-h_{b}}{\|p_{y}-h_{b}\|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.3" class="ltx_p">The gaze score is then the dot product between these unit vectors:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(8)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=d_{x}\cdot d_{y}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=d_{x}\cdot d_{y}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.4" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> approaches <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> when the agent faces the user directly, <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> when looking perpendicular, and <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> when facing away.
Maximizing eye contact corresponds to maximizing <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">During training, we concatenate the per-frame gaze score <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 1}</annotation></semantics></math> with the conditioning <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}=[\mathbf{p}_{y};\mathbf{a};\mathbf{b};\mathbf{g}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐜</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐩</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>𝐛</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>𝐠</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}=[\mathbf{p}_{y};\mathbf{a};\mathbf{b};\mathbf{g}]</annotation></semantics></math> along the channel dimension, and apply classifier-free guidance by dropping <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐠</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}</annotation></semantics></math> with 5 percent probability.
At inference, we specify a target gaze score to control eye contact intensity.
Crucially, guidance gently steers output toward the desired gaze range while preserving natural aversions and variation, yielding realistic and diverse motion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5. </span>Dyadic conversational dataset</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the dyadic conversation subset of the Embody 3D dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">McLean et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
This subset contains around 50 hours captured in a multiview dome.
The conversations cover a vast array of topics, including casual conversations, work discussions, and social interactions.
The demographics are diverse across age groups, genders, and ethnicities.
We use the audio and 3D motion annotations from the dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This is the first dataset to capture 3D spatial proxemics in conversation.
Prior monadic datasets such as Speech2Gesture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ginosar et al., 2019</a>)</cite> and BEAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> offer diverse motion but lack spatial context, capturing a single speaker in isolation.
Existing dyadic datasets such as Audio2Photoreal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Panoptic Studio <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joo et al., 2019</a>)</cite> capture two-person interactions, but participants remain stationary and always face one another.
In contrast, Embody 3D contains scenarios where individuals walk freely, shift positions, and engage in natural, dynamic conversations.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>. </span><span id="S3.T1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison with baselines and ablations (abl.) on 2048 test sequences.<span id="S3.T1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> C = causal, R = real-time. S = speaking (544 seq.), NS = non-speaking (1504 seq.). <math id="S3.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math> higher is better, <math id="S3.T1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math> lower is better. <sup id="S3.T1.6.1.1" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>Reducible to 600 fps without quality degradation.</span></span></figcaption>
