</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our model’s ability to generate realistic, spatially-aware conversational motion.
Following prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, we quantitatively measure realism and diversity against ground truth, and additionally assess gaze alignment to determine whether the agent appropriately orients toward the user within the distribution of natural conversational behavior.
Our results show that our model generates motion competitive with state-of-the-art methods—including non-causal, non-real-time approaches—while being both causal and real-time. <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">For qualitative results, please refer to the Supp. Video</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementation Details</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train our model and run all experiments on an A100 GPU.
For all experiments, we set the sequence length <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=400</annotation></semantics></math>.
Videos are sampled at 30 fps while the audio is sampled at 48kHz.
For the motion representation, we use MHR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferguson et al., 2025</a>)</cite> which allows us to render photorealistic avatars.
For our VAE, we a stride of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=4</annotation></semantics></math>, and the encoder and decoder each have 9 layers with 4 attention heads and a hidden dimension of 256. We set <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1e^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1e^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> for the KL loss.
For the flow matching model, we encode each modality using a learned positional encoding before concatenating them along the channel dimension. We then use rope for temporal positional encoding.
To incorporate the noise timestep, we use AdaLNZero.
We use 4 transformer layers with 4 attention heads and hidden dimension of 1024.
We train with local batch size of 16 across 8 gpu’s.
During inference, we use a cfg of 1.3 to control the conditioning strength.
Since not all methods are autoregressive or causal, we calculate the method’s fps by generating all 400 frames in one go and then dividing the total time taken by 400.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation Metrics</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate motion along five axes:</p>
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FGD</span> (Fréchet Gesture Distance), which measures distributional similarity between generated and ground-truth poses via the Fréchet distance over the vertex positions of the mesh;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FGD<math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\textbf{acc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">acc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\textbf{acc}}</annotation></semantics></math></span>, the same metric computed on acceleration to assess motion smoothness and dynamics;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(3)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Foot Slide</span>, the fraction of frames where feet are near the ground (<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>5 cm) yet moving horizontally (<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>3 cm/s), indicating skating artifacts;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(4)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Wrist Var</span>, the average wrist velocity measuring gesture expressiveness; and</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(5)</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Head Ang.</span>, the mean dot product between the agent’s facing direction and the vector toward the user, quantifying gaze alignment (<math id="S4.I1.i5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> = facing user, <math id="S4.I1.i5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> = facing away).</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We classify each clip as speaking (S) or non-speaking (NS) based on the agent’s audio energy, and report both an overall average and separate S/NS values for each metric to enable analysis across conversational contexts.
For most metrics, the average reflects a weighted mean of the S and NS values.
However, for FGD and FGD<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{acc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>acc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{acc}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the computation differs: the Avg column reports the mean of per-batch Fréchet distances, whereas the S and NS values are each computed by first pooling all clips of that category across all batches, then measuring a single Fréchet distance on the pooled distribution.
This pooling is necessary because individual batches may contain too few clips of one category for reliable covariance estimation.
As a consequence, the per-batch averages systematically exceed the pooled S/NS values due to small-sample-size bias in covariance estimation, and the Avg is not a simple weighted combination of S and NS.
Note that FGD<math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{acc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>acc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{acc}}</annotation></semantics></math> is substantially higher for speaking clips than non-speaking clips, reflecting increased gestural dynamics during speech.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines and Ablations</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since no prior work addresses real-time, spatially-aware conversational motion generation, we cannot directly compare against existing methods.
To ensure a fair comparison, we retrain all prior works on our dataset and motion representation (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. Motion Representation ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>).
We deliberately select foundational architectures—diffusion-based, VQ-based, and hybrid methods—that underpin many recent state-of-the-art systems, rather than task-specific variants with additional modules (e.g., text encoders or domain-specific losses).
This ensures a fair comparison of core generative capabilities.
We compare against:</p>
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random</span>: Randomly samples a motion sequence from the training set, providing a lower bound on performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NN</span>: A nearest-neighbor retrieval baseline that selects motion based on the conditioning inputs.
For audio matching, we use HuBERT embeddings.
We use a library of 2048 motion sequences randomly sampled from the training set and match across the full clip rather than via sliding windows, which yielded better temporal coherence and overall performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tevet et al., 2022</a>)</cite>: A diffusion-based model originally designed for text-conditioned motion generation that has since become a foundation for many subsequent methods that have extended it to support various conditioning signals.
We adapt MDM to use the same conditioning inputs for our domain: agent audio, user audio, and user head trajectory.
It operates non-causally and does not run in real-time.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2P</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>: A hybrid approach combining VQ-based discrete representations with diffusion-based refinement.
It operates autoregressively but is not real-time due to its multi-stage pipeline.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SHOW</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>: A VQ-based autoregressive model designed to generate upper-body, conversational 3D motion from speech.
It employs separate VQ-VAEs for arm and hand movements, followed by an autoregressive generator for full upper-body motion.
With minimal modification to the original architecture, we condition SHOW on agent audio alone to evaluate how existing audio-only methods perform in spatially-aware settings.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also run ablation studies to isolate two key design choices: our motion representation and latent compression via the VAE.</p>
<ul id="S4.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours in Joint Space (IK)</span>: Instead of our Euclidean representation (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1. Motion Representation ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), we encode traditional joint angles with the VAE. Mesh positions are then recovered via inverse kinematics.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours w/o VAE</span>: We remove the causal VAE, directly predicting Euclidean positions from the transformer.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>Quantitative Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tab. <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.5. Dyadic conversational dataset ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes our main results across five evaluation axes.
We organize our analysis by first examining retrieval baselines, then generative baselines, and finally our ablations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Retrieval Baselines (Random, NN)</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The retrieval baselines achieve the lowest FGD scores (<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random</span>: 1.06, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NN</span>: 0.90) since they sample directly from the true data distribution—outperforming <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (1.28) on this metric alone.
However, this advantage is superficial: retrieval methods cannot jointly satisfy all criteria.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random</span>’s gaze alignment score (0.28) is catastrophic compared to <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (0.83) since randomly sampled motion bears no relation to user position.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NN</span> addresses this by jointly matching audio features (HuBERT embeddings) and user position, improving the gaze alignment to 0.59.
While better than <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random</span>, this still falls short of <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (0.83) for two reasons: (1) jointly matching audio and spatial features is non-trivial, as optimizing for one may compromise the other, and (2) no clip in the dataset exactly matches the target user trajectory.
While both retrieval methods achieve near-zero foot sliding (0.01) by copying real motion (matching <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span>), their wrist variance reveals further limitations: <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random</span> (188.1) overshoots GT (137.6) due to context-agnostic sampling, while <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NN</span> (97.0) undershoots as retrieval favors common, less expressive clips.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (105.0) strikes a better balance.
These results highlight a key distinction: while retrieval achieves strong distributional metrics by construction, it is fundamentally limited to what exists in the dataset.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> instead generates novel motion that jointly optimizes for all criteria—achieving competitive FGD (1.28) while dramatically improving spatial awareness (0.83 vs. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NN</span>’s 0.59).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Generative baselines</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate against non-real-time state-of-the-art in the dyadic (two-person) setting, we adapt <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2P</span> to use the same user-aware conditioning as <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span>: agent audio, user audio, and user head trajectory.
When naively adapted to our domain, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> achieves the worst FGD (3.48) among all methods.
Analysis reveals that <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> produces over-smoothed motion: its wrist variance (61.4) is only 45% of <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GT</span> (137.6), indicating severely dampened gestures.
This likely reflects an architecture mismatch: <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> was designed for text-to-motion with coarse action descriptions, not fine-grained audio-gesture synchronization and may favor global motion coherence over local dynamics.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> appropriately matches the ground truth gaze alignment (0.81) perfectly—perhaps due to its non-causal architecture having access to future user positions to allow it to preemptively react accordingly.
In contrast, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> achieves similar gaze alignment (0.83) while operating causally, demonstrating that gaze alignment can be learned without requiring future information.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> also exhibits significant foot sliding (0.11), suggesting that diffusion directly over the euclidean representation actually struggles to maintain physical constraints without a learned latent prior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2P</span> extends <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span> with an additional VQ-based stage: discrete tokens are first generated autoregressively, then refined via diffusion.
This two-stage approach reduces FGD and foot sliding compared to <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MDM</span>.
However, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2P</span> still falls short of <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> across all metrics: higher FGD (2.01 vs. 1.28), lower wrist variance (69.4 vs. 105.0), and weaker gaze alignment (0.71 vs. 0.83).
Qualitatively, we find that A2P’s coarse VQ keyframes can lag temporally, forcing the diffusion stage to correct for misaligned targets.
This results in dampened gestures (lower wrist variance) and temporally offset gaze (lower gaze alignment).
Both diffusion methods also run at only 90 FPS—3<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> slower than <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span>—and their reliance on future context prevents deployment in streaming applications.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18432v1/gaze-eval.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/236;" width="476" height="236" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>. </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We visualize the agent’s facing direction via projected lines (agent: yellow <math id="S4.F5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> red; user: blue <math id="S4.F5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> green). With no alignment <math id="S4.F5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>, the agent’s gaze is more diverse; as we increase <math id="S4.F5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, the agent increasingly turns towards the user.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike the diffusion methods, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SHOW</span> operates causally at 230 FPS, making it the most architecturally comparable baseline to <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span>.
We evaluate it without user conditioning to serve as a monadic (single-agent) baseline.
However, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SHOW</span> struggles even in its original domain—suggesting fundamental architectural limitations even without user conditioning.
On foot sliding, the gap is stark: <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SHOW</span> (0.27) is 27<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> worse than <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (0.01), likely due to its separate VQ-VAEs for arms and hands—originally designed for upper-body motion—which lack body-ground coordination when extended to full-body generation.
On expressiveness, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SHOW</span>’s wrist variance (65.0) falls well below <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (105.0).
Qualitatively, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SHOW</span> produces sweeping gestures but struggles with the rapid, fine-grained motion important for expressive speech—dynamics that <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> captures through its flow-based formulation.
As expected, the largest gap is in spatial awareness: <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SHOW</span>’s gaze alignment (0.61) falls well below <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (0.83).
This highlights a key limitation of audio-only conditioning—the audio signal does not encode user position, so the model cannot learn appropriate orientation.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> addresses this directly through explicit user conditioning, enabling spatially-aware generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablations</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We isolate the contributions of key design choices.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours in Joint Space (IK)</span> replaces our Euclidean surface-point representation with traditional joint angles, requiring inverse kinematics to recover mesh positions.
A core issue is that joint-angle predictions face inherent ambiguity—multiple configurations can produce similar end-effector positions.
This directly impacts metrics that depend on precise positioning: gaze alignment drops from 0.83 to 0.72 (head orientation), and foot sliding increases from 0.01 to 0.03 (foot-ground contact).
The ambiguity may also encourage conservative predictions, which is reflected in wrist variance decreasing from 105.0 to 87.1—the model produces less expressive motion when end-effector targets are uncertain.
These results motivate our Euclidean surface-point approach, which directly specifies end-effector positions without ambiguity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours w/o VAE</span> removes the causal VAE, directly predicting motion from the transformer.
Without the VAE’s learned latent structure, the model must predict high-dimensional motion directly, making it harder to capture the true motion distribution—FGD rises from 1.28 to 1.95.
However, physical plausibility metrics remain stable: foot sliding stays at 0.01 and wrist variance (96.9) remains comparable to <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours</span> (105.0).
This indicates that the VAE’s primary benefit is distributional—matching the motion manifold—rather than enforcing physical constraints, which our Euclidean representation seems to handle.
Inference speed also halves (300 to 150 FPS), as predicting in the compressed latent space is more efficient than directly generating high-dimensional motion.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span>Gaze Control</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate gaze controllability by varying the guidance parameter <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> at test time and applying classifier-free guidance to enforce the desired alignment (Tab. <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.5. Dyadic conversational dataset ‣ 3. Real-time, Auto-regressive Motion Synthesis ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
As shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Generative baselines ‣ 4.1. Quantitative Results ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ SARAH: Spatially Aware Real-time Agentic Humans" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, increasing <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> from 0.0 (looking away) to 1.0 (always facing the user) also increases gaze alignment accordingly (0.56 <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> 0.96). This confirms our method’s ability to explicitly control over agent orientation.
At <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g{=}0.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g{=}0.8</annotation></semantics></math>, which best matches ground truth (0.81), we even outperform the default no-guidance case (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>) with lower FGD (0.92 vs. 1.28) and slightly higher wrist variance.
This suggests that moderate gaze guidance provides useful spatial grounding that improves overall motion quality.
At <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g{=}1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g{=}1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, gaze alignment reaches 0.96 but FGD rises to 1.49, reflecting the trade-off between strict gaze adherence and natural motion variation.
At <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g{=}0.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g{=}0.0</annotation></semantics></math>, gaze alignment drops to 0.56 rather than zero, since complete aversion is rare in the dataset—the agent turns considerably away from the user but still adheres to the learned distribution.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5. </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented the first method for spatially-aware conversational motion, enabling virtual agents to orient toward and react to a moving user <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in real-time</em> while producing natural, speech-aligned gestures.
The architecture pairs a novel causal transformer-based VAE with a flow matching model conditioned on user trajectory and dyadic audio.
Recognizing that gaze preferences vary, we introduce a gaze alignment score steered via classifier-free guidance, decoupling learning from control.
Experiments show state-of-the-art quality at over 300 FPS, outperforming non-causal baselines 3<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> slower.
The causal, real-time nature enables deployment in streaming headset environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our method inherits training data biases: underrepresented spatial configurations or gaze behaviors may generalize poorly.
While we demonstrate controllable gaze, other behaviors—gesture style, locomotion—are not yet controllable.
Extending to multi-party conversations would require architectural modifications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.acknowledgements1" class="ltx_acknowledgements">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_acknowledgements">Acknowledgements.</h6>

</div>

<li id="bib.bib1" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_inproceedings"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Ghorbani <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">et al.</span> (2023)</span>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Supplementary Material</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1. </span>Video Results</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Please refer to <a href="https://evonneng.github.io/sarah/arxiv_videos/full-sequence-d-web.mp4" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">5 minute video</a> for this section.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We start with the problem setup (00:00 – 00:45) for a dyadic conversation between a user and an agent.
Given the user’s 3D position and dyadic audio (from both user and agent), our goal is to generate spatially-aware 3D motion for the agent that aligns with the conversation and moves according to the user’s 3D position.
From the generated motion, we can then render a photorealistic avatar.
<em id="A1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Our model is lightweight and fast enough to enable streaming, allowing real-time interaction with the AI agent on VR platforms.</em></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The streamed results (00:46 – 01:25) demonstrate that our model produces conversationally-appropriate gestures while naturally turning toward the user to signal social engagement.
The agent seamlessly transitions between speaking and listening modes, maintaining dyanamic gestures when speaking, and engaged idle gestures when listening.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our method generalizes across diverse emotional contexts, producing contextually-appropriate body language:
hands on hips and looking down when stressed or rejected (01:26 – 02:00),
lively gestures when excited (02:01 – 02:26),
clenched fists when angry (02:27 – 02:41),
and exaggerated bowing in celebratory agreement (02:41 – 02:57).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure that our model is controllable when it comes to gaze preferences, we also include a gaze score which we can tune at test time.
For lower gaze scores, the agent avoids direct facing the user. For the exact same input conditioning, increasing the gaze score results in more direct facing (02:58 – 03:21).
When we fully drop out the gaze score (<math id="A1.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g=0</annotation></semantics></math>), the agent’s gaze just follows whatever is in-distribution with the training dataset (03:22 – 03:38).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We also compare against existing methods. Compared to MDM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tevet et al., 2022</a>)</cite> our method produces considerably more lively gestures (03:39 – 03:52).
Compared to Audio2Photoreal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, our method produces more realistic motion (03:53 – 04:07).
For Audio2Photoreal, it seems as if the VQ will predict slightly delayed motion which forces the diffusion side to catch up with, which results in distored motion.
Compared to TalkSHOW <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, our method produces less motion artifacts since we predict the full-body motion in a single model (04:08 – 04:22).
Instead, TalkSHOW’s VQ-based approach results in distored wrist motion artifacts and ample foot sliding.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The real-time nature of our model enables fully interactive AI agents in VR (04:23 – end).
We generate dyadic conversations using off-the-shelf LLMs paired with text-to-speech models—here, ChatGPT for dialogue and Kyutai for speech synthesis.
This enables applications ranging from entertainment (e.g., gaming NPCs) to personal assistants.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2. </span>Training Details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide additional training hyperparameters and details not included in the main text.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Optimization</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the AdamW optimizer with <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.999</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.999</annotation></semantics></math>, and weight decay <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The learning rate follows a linear warmup over the first 1,000 training steps, peaking at <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The VAE is trained for 200K iterations before freezing, after which the flow matching model is trained for an additional 300K iterations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data Processing</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a 80/10/10 split for training/validation/test.
During training, we randomly sample a full sequence from the training set and from there, randomly sample a subsequence of length <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=400</annotation></semantics></math> frames.
For test time, we use a sliding window of length <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=400</annotation></semantics></math> and no overlap. We evaluate across the full set and generate 2048 sequences in total.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For audio features, we use HuBERT-Large, which is not fully causal. So at training time, we essentially do have some information leakage.
In order to ensure that it is fully causal at test time, we implement the streaming logic such that we never pass into HuBERT any future frames to avoid this leakage.
Instead, we always implement a sliding window logic where we pass in the current context and then the previous <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T-s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T-s</annotation></semantics></math> frames.
We find that shifting to this fully causal approach at test time does not degrade performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent Dimension</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The VAE latent dimension is <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{z}=256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{z}=256</annotation></semantics></math>.
With stride <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=4</annotation></semantics></math> and sequence length <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=400</annotation></semantics></math>, this produces <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=100</annotation></semantics></math> latent tokens per sequence.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3. </span>Inference Details</h3>

<section id="A1.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Streaming Protocol</h4>

<div id="A1.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For real-time deployment, we generate motion in chunks of <math id="A1.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=4</annotation></semantics></math> frames.
We then keep the last 2 tokens and then remove all the prior ones.
In essence, we generate a total of 8 frames at a time.
As discussed in the main text (), we inpaint the history frames to maintain temporal consistency.
For each chunk, we run using midpoint solver with 4 iterations (8 nfe steps).
In this setting, we are able to achieve 60 fps at test time, which allows us to achieve real-time streaming performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Photorealistic Rendering</h4>

<div id="A1.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bagautdinov et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, a learning based method, to render photorealistic avatars from the generated joint parameter motions.
The model takes as input one frame of facial expression, one frame of body pose, and a viewpoint direction.
We use an off the shelf method to generate facial expression parameters from speech audio.
The model then outputs a registered geometry and view dependent texture, which is used to synthesize images via rasterization.
For further details, please refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bagautdinov et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</article>
</div>
</div>
